cues.say: Component eighteen: timeouts, retries, and the circuit breaker.
Three rules for any call to an outside service, like Stripe: give up after a few seconds, retry with growing waits, and stop calling for a while after repeated failures.
It's a pattern, not a product: a few settings in your HTTP client.
Why does it matter? On game day, Stripe slows from three hundred milliseconds to eight seconds, and each checkout holds a thread while it waits.
Soon every thread is waiting, and even the menu stops loading.
Rule one, the timeout: the longest you'll wait. Say two seconds, then give up and free the thread.
Rule two: retry, waiting longer each time. That's backoff: a hundred milliseconds, then two hundred, then four hundred.
Add a small random wait, called jitter, so clients don't retry in sync. And reuse the same idempotency key, so Stripe charges once.
Rule three, the circuit breaker. It starts closed: calls flow through. After five failures in a row, it opens.
While it's open, calls fail instantly for thirty seconds. Checkout says: try again in a minute.
Then it goes half-open: one test call. If it works, it closes. If not, it opens again.
Wrap every call that leaves your system: payments to Stripe,
texts and email, retried by a worker so the order never waits,
and anything else outside your system, like shipping rates or maps.
Now the pizza shop on game day, with Stripe at eight seconds.
Without the rules, each checkout holds a thread for eight seconds. The threads fill up, and the site stalls.
With them, each call gives up at two seconds and retries once. Five failures in a row, and the circuit opens for thirty seconds.
Checkout says try again in a minute. The threads stay free, and the menu stays fast.
It sits inside the API, around every call to Stripe.
And in the workers, around every text they send.
Two things to watch. Retries add load, so retry only a few times, with backoff.
And only retry what's safe: a payment retried without the same key can be charged twice.
In the interview, say: retries are safe only because the call carries an idempotency key.
